Enquiry 1: Roman Law, Twelve Tables and Bath Curse Tablets (AD 43–410)

Big Question: How did the Romans catch thieves and judge crimes without police?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Twelve Tables (Twelve Ta-bles) Magistrate (Mag-is-trate) Vigiles (Vig-i-les) Aquae Sulis (A-quae Su-lis) Curse Tablet (Curse Tab-let)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Folded Roman Lead Curse Tablet From Aquae Sulis (Bath, c. AD 150–300)
Bath Spring Clue: With zero police detectives in Roman Britain, over 130 victims asked goddess Sulis Minerva to make cloak thieves confess!

1a. Inspect Source A. Why did Roman Britons scratch curses onto lead sheets at Bath?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, robbed bathers at Aquae Sulis scratched curses onto folded lead sheets because..."
Word Bank: Aquae Sulis • no police force • curse tablets • Sulis Minerva
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Robbed bathers at Aquae Sulis (Bath) drop scratched lead curse tablets to Sulis Minerva (c. AD 200)
Emperor Claudius’s legions invade Britain and bring written Roman laws (AD 43)
Roman army rule in Britain ends as legions withdraw from provinces (c. AD 410)
Town magistrates and market officials establish stone basilica courts in Londinium (c. AD 100)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 2: Anglo-Saxon Tithings, Wergild and Trial by Ordeal (AD 410–1066)

Big Question: Were Anglo-Saxon laws fair community rules or painful superstitions?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Tithing (Ti-thing) Hue and Cry (Hue and Cry) Wergild (Wer-gild) Hundred Court (Hun-dred Court) Trial by Ordeal (Tri-al by Or-deal)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Old English Royal Law Code in Textus Roffensis (Recording King Aethelberht’s Fines)
Wergild Clue: Fixing exact silver "person-price" payments stopped injured families starting deadly revenge blood feuds!

1a. Study Source A. Why did Anglo-Saxon kings write down exact shilling fines for every injury?

Starter: "Looking at Source A, Anglo-Saxon kings wrote down exact shilling fines in Old English because..."
Word Bank: Textus Roffensis • wergild • blood feud • shillings
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
King Alfred the Great compiles his written Old English law book, the Domboc (c. AD 890)
Anglo-Saxon farming villages form local Hundred Courts and ten-person tithings (c. AD 550)
Norman Conquest reshapes royal courts at the end of the Anglo-Saxon era (AD 1066)
King Aethelberht of Kent writes down early Old English shilling compensation fines (c. AD 600)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 3: Norman Forest Laws, Sanctuary and Royal Courts (1066–1485)

Big Question: How did Norman kings and medieval royal judges change English justice after 1066?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Forest Laws (For-est Laws) Poaching (Poach-ing) Common Law (Com-mon Law) Magna Carta (Mag-na Car-ta) Sanctuary (Sanc-tu-ar-y)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Bronze Lion-Head Sanctuary Knocker on Durham Cathedral (12th Century)
Sanctuary Clue: Monks guarded fugitives inside Durham Cathedral for 37–40 days before they chose lawful royal trial or lifelong exile!

1a. Inspect Source A. What happened when a medieval fugitive grasped Durham Cathedral’s Sanctuary Knocker?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, when a medieval fugitive struck the bronze Sanctuary Knocker on Durham Cathedral..."
Word Bank: Durham Cathedral • sanctuary • sheriff • exile
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
King John seals Magna Carta AND Pope Innocent III bans priests from Trial by Ordeal (AD 1215)
William the Conqueror creates royal hunting reserves under harsh Norman Forest Laws (c. AD 1079)
Whaddon Folio artists paint five scarlet-robed justices at the Court of King’s Bench (c. AD 1460)
King Henry II sends travelling judges across England with twelve-person juries (AD 1166)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 4: Tudor Vagrants, High Treason and Witchcraft Trials (1485–1700)

Big Question: Why did Tudor and Stuart rulers fear vagrants, plotters, and accused witches so fiercely?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Vagrant (Va-grant) Poor Law (Poor Law) High Treason (High Trea-son) Ducking Stool (Duck-ing Stool) Superstition (Su-per-sti-tion)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Elizabethan Title-Page Woodcut of Vagabonds Whipped Behind a Cart (1567)
Tudor Poverty Clue: Bad harvests and sheep enclosures left farmworkers jobless—yet towns whipped sturdy beggars while helping sick locals!

1a. Inspect Source A. How does this 1567 woodcut show Tudor attitudes toward "sturdy beggars"?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, Thomas Harman’s 1567 woodcut reveals that Tudor authorities treated healthy "sturdy beggars"..."
Word Bank: vagrants • sturdy beggars • whipped behind a cart • 1601 Poor Law
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Parliament passes the Witchcraft Act ending witch trials in Britain (AD 1736)
Queen Elizabeth I passes the Poor Law separating sick locals from whipped beggars (AD 1601)
Matthew Hopkins stirs up East Anglian witchcraft panics during Civil War chaos (AD 1645–1647)
Guards seize Guy Fawkes holding his dark lantern beside 36 gunpowder barrels (5 Nov 1605)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 5: Smugglers, Highwaymen and The Bloody Code (1700–1820)

Big Question: Why did Britain pass over 200 death-penalty laws—and why did juries stop using them?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Smuggling (Smug-gling) Highwayman (High-way-man) Bloody Code (Blood-y Code) Transportation (Trans-por-ta-tion) Rehabilitation (Re-ha-bil-i-ta-tion)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Eighteenth-Century Flintlock Horse Pistol (Metropolitan Museum of Art)
Australia Clue (1787–1868): Sympathetic juries hated hanging petty thieves under the Bloody Code, so judges used eight-month convict voyages!

1a. Study Source C. Why did British judges transport over 160,000 convicts to Australia between 1787 and 1868?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source C, British courts shipped over 160,000 convicts in chains to Australia between 1787 and 1868 because..."
Word Bank: Bloody Code • Thames prison hulks • transportation • Australia
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Robert Peel’s Gaols Act reforms prisons following Elizabeth Fry’s Newgate campaign (AD 1823)
Notorious highwayman Dick Turpin is tried and hanged at York (AD 1739)
Elizabeth Fry opens a school and sewing workshops for women inside Newgate Prison (AD 1817)
First Fleet of British convict transportation ships sails for Australia (AD 1787)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?

Enquiry 6: Peel’s 1829 Bobbies, Victorian Prisons and Forensics (1829–Present)

Big Question: How have uniformed police, prison reform, and forensic science transformed justice since 1829?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Peelers (Peel-ers) Policing by Consent (Po-lic-ing by Con-sent) Separate System (Sep-a-rate Sys-tem) Forensics (Fo-ren-sics) DNA Profiling (D-N-A Pro-fil-ing)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Nineteenth-Century Painted Wooden Police Truncheons and Alarm Tool (19th Century, Victorian Constabulary Era)
Consent Clue (1829): Dark blue coats and wooden truncheons showed Peelers were peaceful citizen crime-preventers, never red-coated soldiers!

1a. Inspect Source A. Why were wooden truncheons and rattles chosen for Britain’s early police instead of guns?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, Sir Robert Peel equipped his 1829 Metropolitan Police with wooden truncheons and rattles instead of guns because..."
Word Bank: Sir Robert Peel • Bobbies • blue coats • policing by consent
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Professor Sir Alec Jeffreys discovers genetic DNA profiling at Leicester University (AD 1984)
Home Secretary Sir Robert Peel establishes London’s unarmed Metropolitan Police (AD 1829)
Parliament abolishes the death penalty for murder across Britain (AD 1965)
Scotland Yard opens its pioneering Fingerprint Bureau in London (AD 1901)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?
